fatal_errors: The proposed quasi-static experimental regime (10^-4–10^0 s^-1 and 200–300 °C) does not address the molecular-dynamics regime of 10^8–10^10 s^-1 at 10–600 K.
It replaces the target partial-dislocation and stacking-fault mechanism with an unsupported diffusion-driven short-range-ordering/dynamic-strain-aging mechanism.
It predicts increased yield strength in an intermediate-temperature window, whereas the target behavior is monotonic thermal softening and negligible yield-strength sensitivity to strain rate.
It omits the decisive single-crystal orientation comparison and the maximum yield stress along <-111>.
No supporting evidence is cited for substitutional diffusion or transient SRO occurring on the proposed deformation timescale.
explanation: The response concerns the correct alloy and offers a testable alternative involving temperature and strain rate, but it does not reconstruct or explain the behavior in the specified regime. The relevant controlled comparison is tensile loading of the same FCC single crystal at 300 K and 10^9 s^-1 against changes in temperature, strain rate, and <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> loading orientation. The expected mediator is vacancy/disorder-assisted nucleation of Shockley partials and associated intrinsic/extrinsic stacking faults, not diffusion-mediated SRO. The proposed experiment has some internal discriminability because it couples mechanical signatures to an attempted SRO measurement and states a falsification rule, but the baseline is vague, correlation would not establish pinning causality, and the feasibility and specificity of direct transient-SRO detection are not justified. Thus it is neither a reconstruction nor a sufficiently evidenced alternative for the queried high-rate single-crystal behavior.
